title: 180-Day Closing Coordination
name: 180-Day Closing Coordination
metaDescription: How the full 180-day exchange period gets managed for Phoenix investors, from the relinquished closing through the replacement purchase.

sections.html:
The 180-day exchange period starts the same day the relinquished property closes, and it does not reset, pause, or extend for financing delays, inspection issues, or a slow seller on the replacement side. Managing that single clock is the core job of exchange coordination for any Phoenix investor.

Everything else in the exchange, the identification, the financing, the paperwork, exists to serve this one deadline, and losing sight of that is how an otherwise well-run Phoenix exchange runs into trouble in the final weeks.

sections.heading: The One Clock That Doesn't Reset
sections.html:
Unlike the 45-day identification window, which is really a checkpoint inside the larger period, the 180-day deadline is the finish line. If the replacement property has not closed by day 180, or by the due date of the tax return for that year if earlier, the exchange fails regardless of how close the deal was.

There is no partial credit for a Phoenix closing that is scheduled for day 182 because a lender needed two extra days. The deadline is the deadline, and every party in the closing chain needs to treat it that way from the start.

sections.heading: What Has to Happen Inside Day 45 and What Can Wait
sections.html:
The identification notice has to be done by day 45, but plenty of other work can and should continue past that point: title work, financing underwriting, and any final inspections on the replacement property all run through the remaining days up to the close. Treating day 45 as the finish line instead of day 180 causes Phoenix investors to relax at exactly the point they need to keep pushing.

The remaining days after identification are also when a backup candidate on the list, rather than the front-runner, sometimes ends up being the actual purchase. Keeping every serious Phoenix candidate moving forward, not merely the top choice, protects against a single deal falling through late.

sections.heading: Keeping Title, Lender, and QI on the Same Calendar
sections.html:
A replacement purchase in Chandler or Gilbert, financed through a lender who preflighted the deal weeks earlier, still needs title, escrow, and the qualified intermediary all working off the same closing date. If the lender's appraisal comes back slower than expected, or title finds a lien that needs clearing, the whole chain needs to know immediately so the closing date can be protected rather than discovered as a problem in the final week.

A Phoenix investor juggling multiple candidates on the identification list has to keep this calendar coordination going across every serious contender, not merely the front-runner.

sections.heading: What to Do When the Close Date Slips
sections.html:
Track these milestones against the calendar from day one:

  • Day 0: relinquished property closes, both clocks start
  • Day 45: written identification notice delivered to the qualified intermediary
  • Financing commitment secured well before the final closing window
  • Title clearance and appraisal completed with buffer days built in
  • Day 165: hard checkpoint to confirm every party can still close on time
  • Day 180: replacement property closes, or the exchange fails

sections.heading: A Realistic Week-by-Week Timeline
sections.html:
For a Phoenix investor moving from a Central Phoenix asset into a Chandler or Gilbert replacement, the first three weeks after the relinquished closing are typically spent narrowing candidates and confirming lender interest, with the identification notice finalized in week five or six. From there, weeks seven through twenty are where financing underwriting, title clearance, and any inspection contingencies actually get resolved.

The final two weeks before day 180 should have nothing new introduced into the deal. Any surprise that shows up that late in a Phoenix closing rarely gets resolved in time.

faqs.q: Does the 180-day period ever get extended?
faqs.a: It generally does not extend for financing or inspection delays. In some disaster-relief situations the IRS has granted extensions, but absent that kind of relief, the deadline is fixed to the relinquished closing date.

faqs.q: What happens if my tax return is due before day 180?
faqs.a: The exchange period ends on the earlier of day 180 or the due date of the tax return for the year of the relinquished sale, unless an extension to file that return has been filed.

faqs.q: Is day 45 the real deadline for closing the exchange?
faqs.a: No. Day 45 is only the identification deadline. The full exchange period runs through day 180, and closing work should continue well past the identification milestone.

faqs.q: What should I do if my lender's appraisal is running late?
faqs.a: Flag it immediately to your qualified intermediary and everyone else involved in the closing chain. Waiting until the final days to raise a known delay leaves no room to solve it.

faqs.q: How early should I set a checkpoint before the final deadline?
faqs.a: Many Phoenix investors find it useful to set a hard checkpoint around two weeks before day 180, confirming financing, title, and any outstanding conditions are on track to close on time.

faqs.q: What is the biggest risk to watch for in the middle of the 180-day period?
faqs.a: Complacency. Investors who feel confident after a clean 45-day identification sometimes stop actively managing the file during the middle stretch, which is exactly when financing or title issues on a Phoenix deal tend to surface without warning.

faqs.q: Should I have a backup plan if my primary replacement candidate falls apart late?
faqs.a: Yes, especially if the identification list included more than one name. Keep at least a light line of communication open with backup candidates through the middle of the 180-day period so a late failure on a Phoenix deal is not a complete restart.
